# Getting started

## Requirements

Everything is installed by [pixi](https://pixi.sh) from the `pixi.toml` in the
repository, so the only prerequisites are pixi and Git.

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
git clone git@github.com:munch-group/itrails.git
cd itrails
```

The repository defines two environments:

`default`
: The workflow itself, plus Jupyter, Quarto and the plotting libraries used by the
  notebooks. This is the environment `pixi run` uses unless told otherwise.

`itrails`
: An isolated environment holding only the iTRAILS package. It is kept separate
  because iTRAILS pins `numpy`, `scipy` and `numba` to specific versions that would
  otherwise constrain everything else. Workflow targets invoke it explicitly, so you
  never have to activate it yourself.

::: { .callout-note }

Because the environments are separate, a workflow target runs its command as
`pixi run --manifest-path <component>/pixi.toml -e itrails itrails-optimize …`. This
works the same way on a laptop and on a cluster, unlike GWF executors, which are
Slurm-only. A parent project that already has iTRAILS installed can override the
prefix with the `run_prefix` argument described in
[Use as a submodule](submodule.qmd).

:::

## Run the example

The repository ships with a one-megabase simulated alignment of four great-ape-like
species (`data/simulated_alignment.maf`), and `analyses.yml` points at it out of the
box. Nothing needs to be downloaded.

On a cluster, select the Slurm backend once and fill in your account in
`analyses.yml`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run gwf config set backend slurm
pixi run gwf run
pixi run gwf status
```

To run on a laptop instead, start a pool of local workers in one terminal:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run gwf -b local workers
```

and submit the workflow from another:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run gwf -b local run
pixi run gwf -b local status
```

::: { .callout-warning }

`gwf status` on the local backend waits for the worker pool. If you see it hang,
the workers are not running — start them in a separate terminal as shown above.

:::

## What happens

For the example analysis the workflow creates nine targets: one split of the
alignment into 500 kb windows, one model fit on the full alignment, a Viterbi and a
posterior decode per window, two concatenation targets, and finally the result
notebook.

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
$ pixi run gwf -b local status
✓ itrails_split_example completed
✓ itrails_optimize_example completed
✓ itrails_viterbi_example_w0000 completed
…
✓ itrails_concat_viterbi_example completed
✓ itrails_concat_posterior_example completed
✓ example_ipynb completed
```

Output lands in `steps/itrails/example/`, one subfolder per step, and
`notebooks/example.ipynb` is executed in place as the last step so it shows the
fitted parameters and the decoded states. See [Output files](outputs.qmd) for what
each file contains.

::: { .callout-important }

`itrails-optimize` is by far the heaviest step: it evaluates the HMM likelihood
repeatedly, and each evaluation costs minutes even on small data. The shipped
configuration uses `n_iter: 100`, which is a few hours on a well-provisioned node
and considerably longer on a laptop. Lower `n_iter` in `config/example_config.yaml`
for a quick smoke test, and give the target many cores for real runs. Decoding, by
contrast, takes minutes per window.

:::

## Using the real great-ape alignment

To run on the published four-species great-ape alignment (183 MB) instead of the
simulated one:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run download-example
```

and point the analysis at it by setting `maf: data/example_alignment.maf` in
`analyses.yml`. The species names in `config/example_config.yaml`
(`hg38`, `panTro5`, `gorGor5`, `ponAbe2`) already match that file.

## Regenerating the simulated data

The shipped alignment is produced by `scripts/simulate_data.py` with
[msprime](https://tskit.dev/msprime/), under a demography that mirrors human, chimp,
gorilla and orangutan: splits at 240,000, 350,000 and 700,000 generations and
ancestral population sizes of 65,000 and 100,000. Fixed random seeds make it
reproducible:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run simulate-example
```

The mutation rate used for the simulation matches the fixed `mu` in the example
configuration, since all iTRAILS estimates are scaled relative to that value.

## Common commands

| Command | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `pixi run gwf status` | state of every target |
| `pixi run gwf status -s failed` | only targets in a given state |
| `pixi run gwf logs <target>` | stdout of a target |
| `pixi run gwf logs -e <target>` | stderr of a target |
| `pixi run gwf clean` | delete output of non-endpoint targets (`--all` for every target) |
| `pixi run gwf touch` | touch output files so everything counts as up to date |
| `pixi run gwf info <target>` | the target's spec, inputs, outputs and options |
| `pixi run quarto render` | build these documentation pages |
